title: Former PM joins list of French presidential candidates reportedly targeted by Russian interference
text:
Three presidential hopefuls have reported Kremlin disinformation efforts against them over the past two weeks.

PARIS — Former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal is the latest in a string of French presidential candidates allegedly targeted by a Russian disinformation campaign.

Attal, the candidate of President Emmanuel Macron's Renaissance party, said on Thursday he had been "a victim" of an electoral "interference" attempt originating from Russia, and that he expected such "destabilization efforts" to increase ahead of France's April 2027 election.

Viginum, the country's agency for fighting online disinformation, confirmed it had detected the operation against Attal and attributed it "with a high level of confidence" to "pro-Russian" disinformation tactics.

Former Prime Minister Édouard Philippe, who is also running for president, was the first to be reportedly targeted last week, before center-left parliamentarian Raphaël Glucksmann, who is expected to run, shared that he had been targeted by a "Russian operation" on Monday.

Attal said on RTL radio on Thursday the smear campaign against him consisted of falsified news reports about his health and policy proposals, which copied the branding of French news outlets. "Russia wants to steal the election from the French," he said.

A 2024 report from Viginum identified a similar "pro-Russian campaign" known as "Matriochka," which involved news and media reports impersonating well-known French outlets.

"Combating foreign interference and protecting our democratic framework are a priority," current Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu posted online on Wednesday. "Several instances of foreign interference targeting candidates have already been detected, and in each case, the individuals were immediately notified."

Martin Ryan had been convicted of espionage charges earlier this year.

Sébastien Lecornu said the deficit would soar to 6.5% without any cost-cutting.

The proposed stronger partnership between Brussels and Ottawa is not directed against anyone else, says the EU Commission.

Philippe Brun said he was “unaware of these allegations” and does not know what he is “accused of.”
